notes.meaning: Under the first covenant, which was God's agreement with Israel through Moses, there were clear rules for worship. God also gave them an earthly sanctuary, a physical tent built in the wilderness. Though it was constructed on earth, it was planned by God to show His desire to dwell near His people.

The tabernacle was a sacred tent divided into two rooms. The first and larger room was called the Holy Place. It contained a golden lampstand to give light, a table, and twelve loaves of holy bread that symbolized God's ongoing fellowship with the twelve tribes of Israel.

A heavy curtain separated the first room from the second, inner room called the Most Holy Place. This inner chamber represented God's immediate presence among His people. The curtain hung as a sacred barrier, showing that ordinary people could not walk directly into God's presence.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern scholars translate the golden censer as the incense altar, explaining that while the altar stood physically outside the curtain, it belonged functionally to the Most Holy Place because its incense was used there.

notes.meaning: The inner room was closely linked to the golden incense altar or censer and held the sacred chest known as the ark of the covenant. Inside the ark were three reminders of Israel's journey: a jar of manna recalling God's daily care, Aaron's budding staff showing God's choice of leaders, and the stone tablets with the Ten Commandments.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern scholars translate the Greek term as the golden altar of incense, explaining that even though it physically sat outside the curtain, its incense and sacred role belonged directly to the Most Holy Place.

notes.meaning: On top of the ark were golden figures of winged heavenly beings called cherubim, whose wings spread over the mercy seat. The mercy seat was the lid of the ark where sacrificial blood was sprinkled to make atonement, which means restoring peace with God by covering sin. The author mentions these treasures briefly so he can turn to their deeper spiritual meaning.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern scholars translate the golden censer as the incense altar, explaining that while the altar stood physically outside the curtain, it belonged functionally to the Most Holy Place because its incense was used there.

notes.meaning: Once the tabernacle was fully set up, the regular priests entered the Holy Place every day to do their work. They trimmed the lamps, burned sweet incense, and replaced the sacred bread each week. These daily duties showed steady devotion, but they were kept strictly within the outer room.

Only the high priest could enter the inner room, and he was permitted to go in only once a year on the Day of Atonement. He never went in without animal blood, which he offered to cover his own sins and the sins the people committed in ignorance. Even the leader of Israel's worship could approach God only with life-blood in his hands.

The Holy Spirit used this strict setup to teach an important lesson. As long as the first tabernacle stood and its system continued, the way into the true presence of God had not yet been revealed. The closed curtain kept people at a distance from God rather than bringing them near.

The earthly tabernacle was a living illustration for that early period. The gifts and animal sacrifices brought by worshipers fulfilled external religious duties, but they could not cleanse the human conscience. They left the inner heart still burdened with the guilt of sin.

These old ceremonies dealt only with dietary rules about food and drink, along with various water washings for the body. They were outward regulations given to guide Israel until God brought about a time of complete reform. That new era arrived when Christ came to change hearts from within.

Christ arrived as the true High Priest of the real spiritual blessings that have now come. He did not serve in a man-made tent set up on earth. Instead, He passed into the greater and perfect sanctuary in heaven, which is not part of this created world.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic teaching holds that Christ continually presents his once-for-all offering to the Father in heaven, and that this same sacrifice is made present upon the altar during the Mass.

notes.meaning: Earthly high priests carried the blood of goats and calves into the inner room year after year, but Jesus entered heaven through His own blood. He entered once for all time, never needing to repeat His offering. By this single sacrifice, He secured eternal redemption, paying the ransom price to set us free from sin forever.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic teaching holds that Christ's one offering is continually presented by Him to the Father in heaven and is made sacramentally present on earth in the sacrifice of the Mass.

notes.meaning: Under the law of Moses, mixing the ashes of a burned red heifer with water cleansed people who had become ritually unclean from touching a dead body. Animal blood and ashes could remove outward contamination so a person could rejoin the worshipping community. These rituals made the body clean, but they could not heal the soul.

If animal blood had power to make bodies outwardly clean, the blood of Christ can do far more. Jesus offered Himself to God as a flawless, willing sacrifice through the eternal Spirit. His blood washes away our inner guilt from dead, sinful deeds so we are free to worship and serve the living God.

Jesus serves as the mediator, the go-between who brings God and humanity together in a new covenant. His death paid the penalty for the sins committed under the old covenant, fulfilling what those earlier sacrifices only pointed toward. Because the debt is paid, everyone whom God calls can freely receive the promised eternal inheritance.

The writer illustrates this truth using the everyday example of a person's last will and testament. A will has no legal power to hand over property while the one who made it is still alive. It takes effect only when that person's death has been proven.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars argue the passage refers to a covenant rather than a will, translating the term as an appointed sacrificial victim that had to be slain over dead animals to confirm the agreement.

notes.meaning: Because solemn agreements and wills require death to take effect, the first covenant at Mount Sinai was also inaugurated with blood. God never established this holy bond through mere words. Sacrificial life had to be poured out to put the covenant into force.

After Moses read all of God's commands to the people, he took the blood of sacrificed animals mixed with water. Using a bundle of scarlet wool and fragrant hyssop branches, he sprinkled both the scroll of the law and all the people. This act showed that the covenant embraced the people and bound them to God's word through atoning blood.

As Moses sprinkled the blood, he announced that it was the blood of the covenant commanded by God. The people committed themselves to obey God's law under the protection of this sacrifice. Jesus used these very words at the Last Supper when He explained that His own blood would establish the new covenant.

In the same way, Moses sprinkled with blood the tabernacle and all the sacred vessels used in worship. Even the holy furniture needed purification because human hands touched it. The sprinkling showed that nothing contaminated by sinful humanity could serve God without atoning blood.

Under the law of Moses, nearly every sacred item was purified with blood, with only rare exceptions cleaned by water or fire. More importantly, without the shedding of blood, there is no forgiveness of sins. True pardon requires that a life be laid down to pay for sin.

The earthly tabernacle was only a copy of the true sanctuary in heaven, so animal blood was suitable to consecrate its tents and tools. The heavenly realities, however, demanded a far greater and purer sacrifice. Christ's perfect offering opens heaven so that cleansed sinners can enter God's presence.

Christ did not enter a sanctuary made by human hands, which was only an earthly sketch of the real thing. He entered heaven itself, right into the presence of God the Father. He is there right now, speaking and acting as our High Priest to represent us before God.

The earthly high priest entered the Most Holy Place year after year carrying the blood of animals, but Jesus does not offer Himself repeatedly. If repeated offerings were needed, He would have had to suffer and die again and again since the creation of the world. Instead, He appeared once for all at the climax of the ages to wipe away sin completely through His own sacrifice.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic teaching explains that the sacrifice of the Mass does not repeat the cross or add a new death, but makes the one, finished sacrifice of Calvary present again in an unbloody manner to apply its graces.

notes.meaning: God has appointed that every person lives on earth, dies a single physical death, and then faces divine judgment. Earthly life gives each person one opportunity to turn to God, with no second chance or repeating cycle of lives after death. Our eternal standing is decided by how we stand with God before we die.

Just as human beings die only once, Christ was offered on the cross a single time to carry away the burden of sin. When He returns the second time, He will not come to deal with sin again, because that work is already complete. Instead, He will bring full, eternal salvation to all who are eagerly waiting for Him.

differ.view: Christ died to bear the penalty of sin for every person born into the world, offering salvation freely to all who believe.
Christ was offered on the cross specifically to bear the sins of the elect, whose complete salvation was purchased and secured.
